title: History, closed
hookLine: the tradition has been broken and has healed, many times

lines: HOLD ALL OF IT AT ONCE.
cards: Why spend so many days on hard history in a daily practice? This block began with that question, and the answer then was simple: the tradition is made of people, and people fail and endure.

You've heard about kings and monks, closed monasteries, wars, exile, killing years, empty niches in a cliff, and broken trust. You've also heard about rebuilding, apology, dignity, chaplains and temples far from home.
Today we close the history, and hold all of it at once.

teach.b: Look at the shape of it. First, the breaks from outside. Rulers protected the sangha and used it.
Governments closed monasteries. Communities were scattered into exile, or nearly destroyed.
Second, the harms from inside. Some Buddhist institutions backed wars. Some monks spoke for hate, while others spoke against it.
Some teachers abused the trust placed in them. This block didn't pretend the tradition only ever suffered things; sometimes its own people did the harm. Third, the healing.
Monasteries rebuilt in India with their old names. A sangha in Cambodia raised again from very few. Doors in China and Mongolia opened again.
Apologies made. Dignity claimed in India by people once called untouchable. Ordination invited back across the sea.
Fourth, why none of this surprises the tradition: anicca, impermanence. Everything made comes apart, institutions included. The teaching doesn't ask anyone to pretend otherwise.
It offers a way to stand while things come apart.

The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in a picture: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm."
History has been a flood more than once.
Again and again, people have built islands in it: a practice kept, a text carried, a door opened.

teach.h: AN ISLAND WHICH NO FLOOD CAN OVERWHELM.
teach.b: Broken, and healed, and broken again. That's the history this path has been telling.

how: Buddhist communities remember hard histories in memorial services, rebuilt temples and teachings on impermanence, and some dedicate merit or loving-kindness to those who carried the tradition through loss.

o: a list of the Buddha's past lives, in order
the chronicles kept only by royal courts
the long story of a tradition broken and healed

games.q: broken and healed: tap the pairs.

s: this block told only harms done to Buddhists by others
it also told harms from inside: institutions that backed wars, monks who spoke for hate, teachers who broke trust.
the teaching expects institutions to come apart too
anicca, impermanence, applies to everything made, including temples and lines of teachers.
gratitude for those who carried the tradition erases the harms
the practice lets gratitude stand next to the harms, not over them.

games.q: the flood of history has swept through your monastery. what does the Dhammapada say the wise do?
o: wait for the flood to pass and do nothing
make an island by earnestness, restraint and control
leave the practice for something safer
games.why: Dhammapada 25: the wise, by rousing themselves, make an island which no flood can overwhelm.

practice: Bring to mind the people who carried this tradition through the hard years, monks walking over mountains, a nun hiding a text, a grandmother in Phnom Penh who still remembered the chants, carvers bent over wooden blocks, and with each breath let a little thanks go toward them.
If your mind drifts to the harms, let them be there too: gratitude doesn't erase them, it stands next to them.

wordCard.voice: History. The long story of a tradition broken from outside and from within, and healed, many times, by people who rebuilt, carried and opened doors again. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. everything made comes apart, institutions too: the reason breaking and healing are no surprise.

carryVoice: Your line: broken and healed. Tomorrow the festival year begins again. I'll be here tomorrow.
